summary:
Grades only take 101 values, so count how many times each grade appears, then write grades 0 to 100 out in
order, each as many times as counted. That's counting sort: O(n + 101) time, no comparisons.

question.md:
Sort up to 10⁵ grades, each between 0 and 100, in **O(n) time**.

- **Many repeats:** 10⁵ grades but only 101 possible values.
- O(n) rules out comparison sorts, which need O(n log n) in general.

think.md:
Grades `[72, 95, 72, 40, 95, 88, 72]`. We don't need to compare grades at all: we know every possible value in advance (0 to 100).
Count each one, then read the counts in order. Sorted: `[40, 72, 72, 72, 88, 95, 95]`.

idea.md: Sort a copy with the language's sort.

lines.text: A general O(n log n) sort.

limits.md: Doesn't meet the O(n) requirement, and compares values even though only 101 different ones exist. Counting them skips comparisons entirely.

idea.md: An array of 101 counters. One pass counts each grade; a second pass over grades 0..100 writes each grade `count[g]` times.

lines.text: One counter per possible grade; the grade itself is the index.
Read the counters in increasing grade order, writing each grade as often as it appeared.
Sorted, without a single comparison between grades.

complexity.md: **Time O(n + R)** with R = 101 possible grades. **Space O(R)** for the counters (plus the output).

steps.text: Grade 40 was counted 1 time(s): write it 1 time(s).
Grade 72 was counted 3 time(s): write it 3 time(s).
Grade 88 was counted 1 time(s): write it 1 time(s).
Grade 95 was counted 2 time(s): write it 2 time(s).

walk.title: Counting sort: one tally per possible grade (0–100), then write each grade out as many times as it was counted.

takeaways.md:
- **Small range of values → counting sort**, O(n + range).
- Comparison sorts can't beat O(n log n) in general; counting sidesteps comparisons by using the values as
  indexes.
- It only pays off when the range is small compared with n (here 101 vs 10⁵).
